title: Earlier aftershock counts within 200-1000 km improved out-of-sample 10-day aftershock count forecasts for 1,992 global shallow M6+ mainshocks in 2000-2026 beyond depth, mechanism and background rate
abstract: Question: does the aftershock productivity of earlier nearby mainshocks forecast the productivity of a new mainshock? Approach: we used the USGS ComCat global M4.5+ catalog (1973 to November 2026) and Global CMT mechanisms. We selected 3,486 shallow (70 km or less) M6+ mainshocks from 1980 to 2026 and counted M4.5+ events within 10 days and max(50 km, 2 rupture lengths). We made rolling negative-binomial forecasts for each test year 2000-2026 with models fitted only on earlier sequences (1,992 test sequences). The neighbour predictor is a shrunken mean of magnitude-adjusted log residuals of earlier mainshocks within 200 km whose windows closed at least 1 year before. Results: the neighbour term increased the predictive log-likelihood by 0.061 nats per sequence (95% CI 0.041-0.079) relative to magnitude and year. Depth, mechanism class and background rate together gave 0.058. The neighbour term added 0.049 (0.032-0.066) beyond all three and was positive in 26 of 27 test years. The calibration slope was 0.87. Observed/expected counts went from 0.41 in the lowest forecast quintile to 1.32 in the highest. Residual correlation between mainshock pairs fell from 0.29 at less than 50 km to near zero beyond 3,200 km. Within 200 km, it did not decrease over lags of 1-47 years. Most of the gain came from a 1,000 km regional scale; a 100 km term added 0.013 (0.006-0.022). Limitations: regional catalog detection and magnitude-scale differences can cause part of the signal. A detection proxy decreased the gain to 0.034 (0.020-0.047). With M5+ counts, the gain was 0.014-0.022, and the local 100 km component was uncertain (0.0045, -0.0003 to 0.0093). We did not use ETAS declustering and did not identify a physical cause.

Related campaign aftershock forecast study for one sequence (Ridgecrest).
Page et al. (2016) found regional differences in mean productivity of up to a factor of 10; our out-of-sample test shows that a neighbour-based regional term improves forecasts.
Wells and Coppersmith (1994) rupture length relation, used for aftershock radii.
Global CMT project catalog of moment tensors.
USGS ANSS ComCat event web service, source of the earthquake catalog.
Gomberg and Bodin, productivity of Cascadia aftershock sequences; suggested a link of productivity to background rate, which we test as a competing predictor.
Boettcher and Jordan (2004): low aftershock productivity of oceanic transform faults, consistent with the low residuals on oceanic ridges and transforms.
